content:
Doris "Dorie" Miller (1919-1943) was an African American sailor who became one of the first heroes of World War II and a symbol of courage in the face of both enemy fire and racial discrimination.

## Early Life
- Born October 12, 1919, in Waco, Texas
- Son of sharecroppers Henrietta and Connery Miller
- One of four sons; nicknamed "Dorie" by his mother
- Was a fullback on his high school football team
- Enlisted in the U.S. Navy in 1939 at age 19

## Naval Service and Racial Context
- Like all African Americans in the Navy at that time, Miller was restricted to the Messman Branch
- Black sailors were only allowed to serve in support roles - primarily as cooks, stewards, and mess attendants
- He was assigned to the USS West Virginia as a Mess Attendant Third Class
- Eventually promoted to Ship's Cook Third Class
- Was the ship's heavyweight boxing champion

## Pearl Harbor Heroism (December 7, 1941)
- When the attack began, Miller helped move his mortally wounded captain to safety
- Despite having no formal training, he manned a .50 caliber anti-aircraft machine gun
- Fired at attacking Japanese aircraft until ordered to abandon ship due to torpedoes and bombs
- Officially credited with shooting down at least one (possibly two) Japanese planes
- His actions were extraordinary given that Black sailors weren't trained for combat positions

## Recognition and Impact
- Awarded the Navy Cross on May 27, 1942 - first African American to receive this honor
- The commendation was presented by Admiral Chester W. Nimitz personally
- Became a national hero and symbol for African American contributions to the war effort
- Used in Navy recruitment drives and war bond tours
- His heroism helped challenge military segregation policies

## Later Service and Death
- Promoted to Cook Third Class in June 1942
- Later served aboard the escort carrier USS Liscome Bay
- Killed in action on November 24, 1943, when the Liscome Bay was torpedoed by a Japanese submarine during the Battle of Makin
- He was 24 years old; his body was never recovered

## Legacy
- In 1973, the Navy commissioned USS Miller (FF-1091), a Knox-class frigate
- In 2020, the Navy named an aircraft carrier (CVN-81) after him - the first carrier named for an African American and an enlisted sailor
- Numerous schools, parks, and facilities bear his name
- Featured on a U.S. postage stamp in 2010
- His heroism is credited with helping pave the way for integration of the armed forces
- Portrayed in several films, including "Tora! Tora! Tora!" (1970) and "Pearl Harbor" (2001)

Miller's courage under fire, despite the racial restrictions of his time, made him an enduring symbol of American heroism and helped highlight the contributions of African Americans in World War II, ultimately contributing to the desegregation of the U.S. military in 1948.
